Plato and Aristotle insisted that only ethical humans could be happy; for the rest of us, happiness comes and goes, as for Mr. Treuer. His was short-lived. He said so here.

People on the left, myself included, tend to lean a bit more towards fear than greed in making investment decisions. I put this down to a general mistrust of capitalism and to the fact that impending-doom bear arguments usually sound smart. Unfortunately for us, it makes for terrible investment decisions.

We all remember Alan Greenspan's prescient coining of the phrase "irrational exuberance" in advance of the dot-com crash.  By now, most people also know that if you bought into the S&P the day he coined that term, you would have done just fine - your investment would have risen a lot in the years before the crash, landed about where you started on the worst day of the crash, and then doubled and re-doubled in the years following the crash.  ..then crashed again in 2007, then doubled and re-doubled again...  It's now about 10X what it was when Greenspan first uttered that phrase.  Will it crash again someday? Sure. Will it give up all its gains by dropping a full 90%? Nope.  

If you're close to retirement, then sure, a heavy bond weighting is a great way to protect your future cash flow from inflation and from market crashes.  For everyone else, the story remains the same: Keep a significant allocation in stocks, and *never* play the fool's game of imagining you can predict when the music will stop. (...but maybe trim your allocation to companies whose value depends on AI services fetching premium fees far into the future...)

The first DUI laws prohibited drunk driving but didn't set a quantitative criterion for intoxication. Legislatures gradually evolved toward per-se laws, so that a person could be convicted of drunk driving--w/o a showing of impaired driving--solely on the basis of his or her blood alcohol level exceeding a minimum threshold--initially 0.15%, then 0.10 to 0.12%, and now 0.08% in most states. Making the job of law enforcement even easier, legislatures also adopted open-container laws, which don't require proof of the consumption of any alcohol, but also don't carry the same penalties as a DUI violation.

Will state legislatures treat marijuana use differently from how they treat alcohol use? I guess it all will come down to the various lobbies--of law enforcement, of the alcohol industry, of the marijuana industry, and of the user communities, and, of course, the public at large.

From our hometown Mamaroneck Train Station, we boarded MetroNorth’s New Haven Line down to Harlem-125th Street and then transferred to the Hudson Line up to Croton-Harmon. There we boarded Amtrak’s Lake Shore Limited for an overnight trip on a Viewliner Roomette to Chicago’s Union Station, passing through New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois. In Chicago, we spent one night in a hotel (near the station) before boarding Amtrak’s Southwest Chief, traveling for 3 days and 2 nights in a Superliner Roomette through Illinois, Iowa, Missouri, Kansas, Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, and finally California. We disembark the Southwest Chief in Fullerton, CA and then boarded Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner down to San Diego.

It was so much fun! Hopefully my daughter will remember it for years to come. 

(My wife flew out to San Diego to meet us. Our trip took us 5 days. Her’s took just over 5 hours.)

It's funny to come from such a different culture and yet still understand exactly what you're feeling.

My grandparents lived on a small rural property in the metropolitan area of Rio de Janeiro. It was only about 30 km away, but back in the 1980s and 1990s that was enough for their grandchildren to have a taste of country life. The house was huge. My grandparents no longer kept livestock, but my grandfather still grew corn, sugarcane, pigeon peas, and a few other crops.

The property had dozens of fruit trees, including three or four varieties of bananas and mangoes. There were some native Brazilian fruits you've probably never heard of, such as acerola and jabuticaba, as well as tropical fruits originally from Asia that are commonly found throughout Brazil, like jackfruit and cajá. There was also a small stream where we used to fish. We played volleyball and soccer with friends and relatives who lived nearby.

My grandparents both passed away within a year of each other, between 2000 and 2001. I still spent a few nights there afterward whenever I went to visit my uncles, who also lived in the area. It was very difficult. After my grandmother died in 2001, my brother could never bring himself to go back inside the house. It was just too painful.

I think my father and my uncle sold the property sometime in 2002. Sometimes I think it would be nice to still have that place to go back to, but deep down I think they made the right decision.

Thanks for the article.

For me the toughest market period was between 1969 and 1982, when the market indices, in real dollars, plunged over 50%. Since then the gain has been major though with some setbacks.

I agree with the need to have some liquid assets. In addition to a stock portfolio with about a 3% dividend, I have a significant accumulation of cash in a money fund $3.4%. A major reason that I don’t hold long bonds is that, in an inflationary period, the payback of a 10 year federal bond would be significantly less than their purchase price. You will also have better luck in selecting assets that don't incur state taxes.  That gets very tricky with a lot of money market funds that invest in things that sound like government issue but which don't get you a state tax exemption.  Strips for example.

https://mises.org/mises-wire/high-cost-automated-flock-camera-surveillance-state

a slice:

"Flock cameras, and the online surveillance network behind them, offer many ways for law enforcement officials, and other government bureaucrats, to abuse their access to information about the personal lives of the taxpayers. 

There are very few controls on how police can use the surveillance databases that underlie the data collection. Records have shown that police can put out a “Flock alert” to track a private vehicle without the vehicle owner or operator being the target of any legitimate investigation. 

Many people wrongly think that these are just ordinary surveillance cameras that can be accessed piecemeal by actual humans. In reality, these are AI-assisted automated systems designed to provide easily-accessed tracking data on the movements of any American who drives a car on America’s streets.

These low frequency (in a human life span terms) high impact events in mountainous regions such as the Himalaya are nothing new and should be an expectation independent of human induced climate change. In the same region, there was a much larger documented mountain avalanche event in 1190 (Lavé et al. 2023 Nature). A similar mountain avalanche in 1970 Yungay, Peru destroyed the town and several villages with something like 30,000 dead (Eriksen et al. 1970 USGS). There are many other examples.

These disaster events in mountainous glaciated terranes have happened and will happen again and again.

comments.name: Penelope Green

Jerome Smith was heroic in so many ways. As a young Freedom Rider, he undertook two missions, one that ended in jail, and a second that nearly killed him. Like most of the riders, he was so young, just 22, but he had extraordinary discipline, both from the nonviolent practices that were integral to the Congress of Racial Equality, the civil rights organization he had dropped out of college to join, and the quiet activism he learned from his parents, who flouted Jim Crow “laws” on a daily basis. He always credited his mother, Leona Smith Sampier, for his strength and intellectual growth. “I’m a momma’s boy,” he liked to say. It makes sense he founded a children’s organization, Tamborine and Fan, in his hometown of New Orleans. Black history and civic engagement were a huge part of its ethos. His daughter Farin Smith recalled the day he brought 100 or so Tamborine and Fan day campers to “sit-in” in mayor Moon Landrieu’s office when the city would not supply buses to take the children to a water park. Needless to say, the mayor relented.

“Nobody said no to Jerome,” Farin Smith told me. “Every politician learned that lesson.” 

It was an honor to learn about this extraordinary man!

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen

We are experiencing a very non linear increase of local and regional climate-related impacts surprising many scientists by how soon they are occurring: heat waves, droughts, wildfires, floods, stronger storms, etc.

This is in large part because ice melt, which reduces heat reflectivity, is causing the Arctic to warm around 4 times the rate of the whole planet and the decreased horizontal temperature gradient between the Arctic and the rest of the world has helped cause the northern polar jet stream to slow, and get stuck in wavy patterns.

These patterns bleed heat north and cold south, and cause weather systems to persist (like the heat wave that spread fire that incinerated Lytton, British Columbia a few years ago).

Also for every degree C rise in temperature the atmosphere can hold 7 percent more moisture, an exponential increase. Hence the “rain bombs” we’ve been seeing around the world.

As we get flooded by this from above the rate of sea level rise is accelerating and maximum storm strength is increasing.

There’s some adapting that we have to do to the changes already in the pipeline, but it wouldn’t take us long to make the changes too big to adapt to.

comments.body:
Suno’s use of copyrighted material does not fall under the “fair use” doctrine, which evaluates the use under four metrics:

1) Purpose and character: whether the use is for non-profit or educational, versus commercial, purposes. Because Suno is using  these songs to generate profit for itself, it fails this test.
2) Nature of the work: whether the use is of factual or published works rather than highly creative works or works intended for private use. Although these songs are played in public, they require the payment of royalties and are creative in nature, so Suno fails this test as well.
3) Amount used: fair use is more likely to apply when only a small part of a piece of work is used, rather than its entirety. Here, Suno is not just using a part of a song by these artists, it’s using their entire song catalogs to imitate their style.
4) Market effect: protects the creator of an original work when the use will harm the current or potential market for that work. Although it is unlikely that the public will prefer an AI-generated facsimile to the original artist, Suno’s actions do cheapen the value of the original work and the artist’s style, so this factor would not likely be able to override the use of the artists’ work without their permission.

Another interesting thing about Hosono is that his grandfather, Masabumi Hosono, was one of the passengers on the Titanic. For decades, he was derided as a coward for having survived instead of going down with the ship; for a long time, this was something the family never spoke about. It was only after the release of James Cameron's film that his reputation was redeemed.

Something this piece overlooks is that Hosono has also long been active as a producer and arranger. articles.summary: For the first time in a year, the U.S.-Mexico border partly reopened to cattle imports following a screwworm infestation across the region. The battle against the flesh-eating fly has only just begun deep in Mexico.
